newsitem.title: INDIA: India to eliminate subsidy on gas in three years.
newsitem.headline: India to eliminate subsidy on gas in three years.

text.p: India plans to eliminate subsidy on natural gas in three years to bring it at par with global gas prices, a senior Petroleum Ministry official said on Friday.
"Subsidy on natural gas prices will be gradually lowered over the next three years to bring it in line with international prices," the official, who asked not to be identified, told Reuters.
The decision was taken by a committee of senior officials of petroleum, finance, power and fertiliser ministries on Thursday, the official said.
A formal note based on the committee's recommendations will be forwarded to the Union Cabinet for approval within a fortnight, officials said.
The committee has decided that price of natural gas will be linked to international price of low sulphur fuel oil.
It has been recommended that from September this year, prices of natural gas at delivery points should be hiked to 2,050 rupees ($57.4) per million cubic metres (MCM) from the present 1,850 rupees.

The official said the committee was of the view that price of gas supplied through India's main HBJ (Hazira-Bijaipur-Jagdishpur) gas pipeline should be increased to 3,200 rupees per MCM from 2,700 rupees.
The committee said prices should be equated with 65 percent of the ruling international price of low sulphur fuel oil by 1998/99 (April-March).

In the third year, the price of natural gas would need to be fixed at 75 percent of the global price of low sulphur fuel oil, the official said. This would bring it in line with global practice of indexing natural gas prices with fuel oil prices.
The state-run Gas Authority of India Ltd will be paid by the government 1,150 rupees per million cubic metres as cost of transporting the gas from producing fields to industrial consumers.
Gas producers state-run Oil and Natural Gas Corp and Oil India Ltd will be given the surplus revenue generated to develop gas fields, the official said.
Compression of the time frame to deregulate gas prices will also send signals to private producers to increase their investment in developing gas fields, the official said.
The committee also ruled out a differential pricing of gas for power and fertiliser sectors which have been demanding lower prices since they cater to needy sections.
